newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Angry Yugoslav arms workers march on Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: Angry Yugoslav arms workers march on Belgrade.

text.p: Scores of furious workers calling the government "thieves" and demanding a revival of Yugoslavia's biggest arms company arrived in Belgrade on Thursday having walked over 120 kilometers (75 miles) from the central Serbian town of Kragujevac.
Workers demanded repayment of some $72 million owed by the government for earlier weapons deliveries, late wages, new programmes to revive production and funds from the Serbian Develoment Fund.
"They should first return what they stole from us," the plant's independent trade union secretary Dragutin Stanojlovic told the angry crowd to chants of "Thieves, thieves, thieves".

More than 100 marchers of Zastava Namenska set off on Tuesday morning and were joined in the capital by several hundred others who arrived in buses, including arms factory workers from Uzice and Cacak.
Their plans to hold a rally outside the Serbian government were prevented by police who cordoned off the area and moved the protest to another central square.

Suffering from lack of cash and loss of markets like the rest of the economy, the plant's prospects for reviving production are bleak especially following an international arms reduction accord which Yugoslavia signed in 1995.

Although the plant, once a major export earner, carried on production during the 1991-95 wars in ex-Yugoslavia, it lost valuable foreign markets under a U.N. trade embargo clamped on Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, in 1992.
"We are hungry, thirsty and barefoot, but we still must pay our electricity bills or they will cut us off," said Milica, a 40-year old woman who has worked in the factory for 20 years.
Although the exact number of workers is a "state secret" a trade union official at the protest told Reuters: "There are between 5,000 and 7,000."

"More that half are on paid leave, half have no prospects and they say we have preserved the factory. But all we have preserved are the walls and the iron, not the people," said Zoran Nedeljkovic, Namenska independent trade union president.
"I believe Serbia's workers will not tolerate much longer this poverty and deprivation. We will not allow anyone to trample our honour any longer," Stanojlovic said.

The 144-year-old factory survived Turkish rule, World War One, the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, World War Two and 50 years of Communism, but since the Socialists came to power it has become unbearable for workers in this country, Nedeljkovic said.

Kragujevac, a major industrial town, saw mass workers protests rallying up to 10,000 people last year, including Zastava arms workers who protested for an hour each day outside the Kragujevac city council for nearly two months.

The protest drew only slight support from Belgraders, some of whom turned out with whistles and trumpets reminiscent of three month of protests in Belgrade last winter against local election fraud. -- Belgrade newsroom +381 11 311 4305
